input.headline: The flicker of the ceiling lights matches the national grid record at 11:45:38 UTC on Sunday 8 November 2026, so the stated start time holds.
findings: The scene is a dark room lit only by ceiling strip lights. No on-screen clock is visible, so the time had to come from the electricity signal.
The flicker of the lights carried a strong mains-frequency signal, usable in about 71% of the recording. The mains hum in the audio was too weak to use (19% usable), so only the video was used.

Searching 2 hours either side of the stated time on the GB grid record (Elexon, 15-second resolution) gave one clear best match. It starts at 11:45:38 UTC with a score of 0.96 out of 1. The next-best time that day scored only 0.80.
Sharpness: the match falls off within seconds of 11:45:38 (0.82 at ±10 s, 0.34–0.52 at ±60 s). This means the time is pinned down tightly.

The first and second halves of the recording were matched separately. They point to 11:45:39 and 11:45:36, which agree within the precision of the reference data. That is consistent with one continuous recording and gives no sign of splicing.
Other days: the best matches on 5–11 November scored at most 0.84, well below the 0.96 match on 8 November.
input.what_it_means: The electricity signal in the video independently confirms that it was recorded starting about 11:45:37–11:45:38 UTC on 8 November 2026. Unlike metadata or a device clock, this signal can't easily be changed after the fact. The timing evidence supports the account of the person who supplied the recording. It only establishes when the recording was made, not what it shows or who made it.
next_steps: The start time can be treated as independently corroborated for this recording.
If a higher-precision check is needed (for example, if seconds matter), re-run the match against NESO 1-second grid data for November 2026 once it is published.
Keep the original file and how it was handed over on record, so this finding can be tied to the exact file examined.
